framing: Each entry is the family's open working theory, not checked, shown with what cuts against it.

theories.title: The Williams family held Tŷ Mawr as freeholders, and the holding was reduced parcel by parcel
theories.summary: The family's central working theory. The Williams family may have held Tŷ Mawr and land around it as a family of standing in the parish, owning as well as occupying it, rather than as tenants of the lord of the manor. On this reading the holding was reduced parcel by parcel over generations, and later records came to describe the family's occupation as a tenancy, then as permissive, then as adverse.

evidence_for.note: 1824 Stewart survey: “Cedfin or Ty Mawr Farm”
c.1841 tithe: John Williams on 36 numbered plots

against: The c.1841 tithe enters John Williams as occupier of the 36 plots, not as landowner: the landowner column names the Marquess of Bute for 33 of them and the Revd James Evans (glebe) for 3.
The 1824 survey is the Bute estate's own survey of its lands, and it includes the farm.
Cardiff Records (vol. 2) records the manor of Llandough as bought by the Earl of Bute in 1793, after Tewkesbury Abbey, the Crown's grant of 1543 and the Herberts and their heirs.
No deed, will or settlement putting the house in Williams ownership has been found yet.
The 1987 Court of Appeal decided possession for the registered side, on the record then before it.
theories.test: The free tenants named in the 1545 Llandough rent-roll and the 1596 manorial survey (both manors then had free tenants as well as demesne and copyhold); the schedule of the 1793 sale of the manor to the Earl of Bute, to see whether the house was demesne or a free tenant's holding; and any Williams deed, will or settlement for Llandough before 1824.

theories.title: Bounced-notice theory
theories.status_label: Tested · the records so far do not match it
theories.summary: Some recipients of the family's record-preservation notices might be able to read emails that show as bounced on the sender's side, so that a bounce would leave room to write later that no notice arrived, and to date any disposal of records before the first notice they accept.
against: All four bounces to these recipients (February, June, August and September 2026) were refused by the recipient's own mail server at the address check, before the message text is sent, so the text never reached them.
Each bounce went to a closed or wrong address; each recipient had a working address that accepted the notices.
The preservation notice of 28 September 2026 did not bounce for any of these recipients.
Bounces are common in the family's mailbox overall, across many unrelated recipients.
No recipient has dated a disposal of records to a time after a bounce.
theories.test: A subject access request for each recipient's mail-gateway logs (accepted, refused, quarantined) for the family's emails; a message trace for the 28 September notice.

theories.title: First “not held” replies can understate what a body holds
theories.summary: Two bodies first replied that they held nothing in scope, then produced a record after a challenge or a fresh look.

evidence_for.title: Amgueddfa Cymru – Museum Wales · reply of 2026-08-25

against: In both cases the holder corrected the reply itself; an ordinary search error explains it.
Two cases do not make a pattern.
theories.test: Track every “not held” reply for a later find, and ask each body for the search terms it used.

theories.title: A 1928 end to rent would have barred any action to recover the house about 1940
theories.summary: The family's c.1974 statement records that the last rent was paid in 1928. If the house parcel stopped being let then, any right to recover it accrued in 1928 and was barred about twelve years later, before the 1949 re-grant and the 1955 date the 1987 court used.
against: The 1987 judgment records rent arrears in the mid-1930s and late 1940s, which implies a tenancy continuing after 1928.
The 1928 rent receipt has not been found; only a later diary reference is held.
theories.test: The estate rental books and plan book for c.1938–44, and any 1928 estate rental that drops the house parcel.

theories.title: Bodies with records at stake answer on process, not substance
theories.summary: In the request correspondence (913 emails, 57 bodies), the bodies that hold registration, demolition and burial records reply about process and rarely address the events asked about, while archives and museums with nothing at stake explain their searches in detail.

evidence_for.title: Vale of Glamorgan Council · reply of 2026-06-02
HM Land Registry · reply of date not yet read

against: Narrow searches, old files and routine destruction explain many short replies without any intent.
The counts come from our own coding of the emails, which no one else has checked.
theories.test: Internal reviews and regulator decisions that require a body to show the search it made.

theories.title: The 1974 letters did the work of an enforcement that was running out of time
theories.summary: Leave to enforce the 1962 possession order was given in September 1974, about 12 weeks before the order's 12-year anniversary. The warrant was withdrawn on 31 Oct 1974 for lack of notice, and the licence letters are dated the same day. The Court of Appeal later held that those letters turned the occupation into a licence.
against: The House of Lords held in 1999 (Lowsley v Forbes) that the 12-year limit on actions on a judgment does not stop execution itself, so the clock may not have bound anyone in law.
theories.test: The 1974 leave application and its sworn statement (MR-0012). The county court replied that it holds nothing because of age (MR-0014).

theories.title: Twelve-year gaps between a refused arrangement and a registration
theories.summary: On three lines of the land’s history (woodland, green, house), a permissive arrangement the family refused was followed by a deed or registration in another name roughly 12 years later: 1949 to 1961, 1958/9 to 1970, 1974 to 1983. Twelve years is the limitation period for recovering land.

evidence_for.note: 1961 deed recited on the woodland title

against: Across all landholder moves from 1928 to 1988 there is no regular 12-year rhythm; the gap holds per line, not as a cycle.
A green registration rests on 20 years' use as of right, not 12 years' possession.
Only three lines, and the start dates were picked after the pattern was noticed.
theories.test: Any record showing whether the occupier was told at each step (missing-records MR-0007, MR-0010, MR-0017, MR-0012, MR-0020, MR-0021).
